Self
self
n. and pron. (one's own person; used in the Authorized Version chiefly in the emphatic mine own self, his own self, thine own self)
Saxon self. In the Authorized Version the bare noun almost always appears in an emphatic possessive phrase, and the two most important of those phrases belong to Christ — what He could not do of His own self, and what He bore in His own body.

Biblical Definition

The word's two great occurrences are both about the Son. First, His dependence: “I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me” (Joh 5:30). The eternal Son, equal with the Father, says in His incarnate mission that He acts from no independent self-will. That is the pattern of every creature's proper relation to God, held perfectly by the only One who could have claimed otherwise. Second, His substitution: “Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed” (1Pe 2:24). Peter piles up the possessives — his own self, his own body — because the whole doctrine of the atonement stands on the personal, bodily, substitutionary bearing of sins that were not His. Then the same phrase in prayer, reaching back before creation: “glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was” (Joh 17:5). Paul uses it of judgment: “yea, I judge not mine own self” (1Co 4:3) — even his own verdict on himself is not final, for he that judgeth him is the Lord. And in Philemon, of a debt: Philemon owes Paul “even thine own self besides” (Phm 1:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines self as having its own or a single nature, as in self-love; and as expressing the individual person, in the emphatic forms myself, himself, thyself.

expand to see more

SELF, pron. Having its own or a particular nature; united to a pronoun to express emphasis or distinction.

1. It is used to express the individual, as distinguished from all others.

2. In composition, self denotes something done by one's self, or of one's own nature; as self-denial, self-love, self-evident.

SELF-DENIAL, n. The denial of one's self; the forbearing to gratify one's own desires or appetites.

Key Scripture

1Pe 2:24 — "Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed."

John 5:30 — "I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me."

John 17:5 — "And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was."

1Co 4:3 — "But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man's judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self."

Modern Corruption

The self has become the reference point of all value; Scripture makes it the thing to be denied and Christ the one who bore our sins in His own body.

expand to see more

The modern religion of the self — self-esteem as the root of health, self-actualization as the goal of life, self-expression as the highest honesty, the authentic self as the final authority — is a complete anthropology, and it is not the Bible's. Our Lord's terms are the exact reverse: if any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whosoever will save his life shall lose it. This is not a call to self-hatred, which Scripture nowhere commands; the second great commandment assumes a man loves himself and tells him to love his neighbour that way. It is a call to dethrone the self as the reference point, which is a different thing entirely and a great deal harder.

The gospel's answer to the question of the self's worth is better than anything the self-esteem literature can offer, and it comes from outside. A man's value is not a verdict he passes on himself — Paul says even his own verdict does not count, I judge not mine own self — but the estimate of the One who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree. Nothing a person can say about himself, high or low, weighs against that transaction. And the freedom of it is enormous: a man who has stopped adjudicating his own worth can finally get on with loving his neighbour.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek autos (G846), self, the same, he himself; emautou (G1683), of myself; aparneomai (G533), to deny utterly — the verb of self-denial.

expand to see more

Greek autos (G846) — self, himself; 1 Peter 2:24, his own self — the emphatic pronoun carrying the personal substitution.

Greek emautou (G1683) — of myself, from my own initiative; John 5:30, I can of mine own self do nothing.

Greek soma (G4983) — body; 1 Peter 2:24, in his own body on the tree — the atonement is bodily.

Greek anaphero (G399) — to carry up, to bear up, as a sacrifice to an altar; the verb behind bare our sins.

Greek aparneomai (G533) — to deny utterly, to disown; Luke 9:23, let him deny himself — the same verb used of Peter denying Christ.

Usage

"“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree”."

"“I can of mine own self do nothing” — said by the Son."

"“I judge not mine own self” — even Paul's verdict on Paul is not final."
